entry.title: An emergent property of matter
entry.content:
In May 2024, on the All-In podcast, Sam Altman said something that Karen Hao quotes in Empire of AI (chapter 17) as an example of his “unusual degree of hype”. It feels to him, he said, “like we just stumbled on a new fact of nature or science or whatever you want to call it”. He hedged, “I don’t believe this literally but it’s like a spiritual point”, and then said it anyway:

intelligence is just this emergent property of matter and that’s like a rule of physics or something.

Hao places it in a run of unusually boastful interviews that spring, which she reads as a sign that Altman was anxious: GPT-4o launched that month, lawsuits were piling up, and in the middle of May Sutskever and Jan Leike left the company. I do not read the sentence as hype. It is the most important thing anyone at OpenAI has said, and I share the conviction, including the part he hedged.

The claim, stated plainly: intelligence is not a gift that only brains received. Arrange matter so that it predicts its surroundings, put it under pressure to predict better, give it enough scale, and intelligence appears, the way temperature appears from moving molecules and a glider appears in Conway’s Game of Life. The evidence is now on several substrates at once. Neurons evolved it. Neurons in a dish learned to play Pong in a few minutes, the experiment behind my small simulation Hotaru. Transformers trained to predict the next word learned to reason. None of these were told what intelligence is; it came out of the arrangement.

“A rule of physics” overstates it, and Altman says so himself. There is no equation, and I do not know the conditions under which it holds. The counter-arguments are serious: that a model trained on text only rearranges what people wrote (Bender and Gebru’s stochastic parrots, which Hao also covers), or that intelligence needs a body and a world to act in, which I lean towards in in vivo, not in vitro. But both arguments are about which arrangements are enough, not about whether matter can do it.

The spiritual point is the part I care about most. If intelligence is something the universe does whenever matter is arranged in the right way, then minds are not an accident on one planet but a regularity, and building them is less like inventing a machine and more like discovering a law. That is a quasi-religious conviction, and I hold it as one. It is also, I think, why the people who build these systems talk about them with a seriousness that sounds like faith to everyone else. They are not wrong to feel it.

More on the book in my review, An Empire of People, and on emergence in Hassabis’s simulated worlds in Win Everything, Control No One.

References

  • Karen Hao, Empire of AI (2025), chapter 17, “Reckoning”. Hao gives the All-In podcast, May 2024, as the source.
  • Brett J. Kagan et al., “In vitro neurons learn and exhibit sentience when embodied in a simulated game-world”, Neuron 110(23), 2022.
  • Emily M. Bender, Timnit Gebru, Angelina McMillan-Major, and Margaret Mitchell, “On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?”, FAccT 2021.

entry.title: Something closer to a religion
entry.content:
Karen Hao opens Empire of AI with two epigraphs. One is a passage from Sam Altman’s blog in 2013. He had heard a saying from Qi Lu: successful people create companies, more successful people create countries, and the most successful people create religions. Altman drew his own conclusion: the most successful founders “are on a mission to create something closer to a religion”, and at some point a company turns out to be the easiest way to do it.

Hao comes back to it in chapter 18, where she argues that OpenAI’s mission works as a formula for empire: it gathers talent, it gathers capital, and it is vague enough to be reinterpreted at will. In chapter 10 she writes that the people who fear AGI and the people who long for it preach from the same bible. For her, the religious quality of the AI labs is the warning sign.

I read the same sentence as a forecast, and an accurate one. A company has always held people together with two things: what it pays them for and what it lets them believe. For most of industrial history the first carried the weight. The work was the reason to show up, the wage was the reason to stay, and the mission statement was decoration. If AI makes a great deal of human work cheaper, the first bond weakens. What is left to hold a group of people together is the second: a shared idea of what they are building and why it matters.

That is not new. Monasteries, guilds, universities, and the early labs of the nuclear age were held together this way, and they built things no wage alone would have bought. The OpenAI that Hao describes runs on the same fuel: people who took less money than Google offered because they believed in the mission, and who threatened to leave together when they thought it was in danger. Altman put a line from Admiral Rickover on the office walls for the same reason (One person can make a difference).

Hao is right that a belief can be bent to serve power, and that a vague mission can be reinterpreted to justify almost anything. That is the risk of every religion. But the answer is to look at what the faith builds and whom it serves, not to wish companies were held together by wages alone. I expect more of them to look like this, not fewer, and I share some of the faith myself: An emergent property of matter.

More on the book in my review, An Empire of People.

References

  • Karen Hao, Empire of AI (2025), epigraph, chapter 10, “Gods and Demons”, and chapter 18, “A Formula for Empire”.
  • Sam Altman, Successful People, blog post, March 7, 2013.
